title: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
short_intro: Forced oscillations occur when a mechanical system is subjected to a continuous periodic driving force. The system ultimately oscillates at the frequency of the external driver rather than its own natural frequency.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of forced oscillations, qualitative understanding of resonance, amplitude and frequency relations, and basic examples.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical derivation of the steady-state amplitude and phase angle, sharpness of resonance, quality factor (Q-factor), and power absorption.

prerequisites: Damped harmonic motion and damping coefficient
Differential equations of second order with constant coefficients

concept_notes.heading: Differential Equation of Forced Oscillations
bullets: A system of mass m subject to restoring force -kx, damping force -rv, and external periodic force F_0 cos(omega t) is governed by m(d^2x/dt^2) + r(dx/dt) + kx = F_0 cos(omega t).
Dividing by m yields d^2x/dt^2 + 2gamma(dx/dt) + omega_0^2 x = (F_0/m) cos(omega t), where gamma = r/(2m) is the damping factor and omega_0 = sqrt(k/m) is the natural angular frequency.
The complete solution consists of a transient part (which dies out due to damping) and a steady-state part (which persists at the driving frequency omega).

concept_notes.heading: Steady-State Response and Phase Lag
bullets: In the steady state, the displacement is given by x(t) = A cos(omega t - phi), where A is the steady-state amplitude and phi is the phase lag of the displacement behind the driving force.
The phase angle phi is determined by tan(phi) = 2gamma omega / (omega_0^2 - omega^2).
At low driving frequencies (omega << omega_0), phi approx 0. At resonance (omega = omega_0), phi = pi/2. At high frequencies (omega >> omega_0), phi approaches pi.

concept_notes.heading: Amplitude Resonance
bullets: The amplitude of forced oscillations is A = (F_0/m) / sqrt((omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4gamma^2 omega^2).
Amplitude resonance occurs when the denominator is minimized with respect to omega, giving the resonant angular frequency omega_r = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2gamma^2).
For very light damping (gamma approx 0), the resonance frequency coincides with the natural frequency omega_0.

concept_notes.heading: Quality Factor and Sharpness of Resonance
bullets: The Quality factor (Q) measures the sharpness of resonance and is defined as Q = omega_r / (2gamma) approx omega_0 / (omega_2 - omega_1), where omega_2 - omega_1 is the full width at half maximum of the resonance power curve.
A high Q-factor implies very light damping, a narrow resonance peak, and a large amplitude at resonance.
At resonance, the maximum amplitude is A_max = F_0 / (2m gamma omega_r) = Q(F_0 / k).

derivations.title: Steady-State Amplitude and Phase Angle Derivation
derivations.conditions: Assumes steady-state solution x(t) = A cos(omega t - phi) for the equation d^2x/dt^2 + 2gamma(dx/dt) + omega_0^2 x = (F_0/m) cos(omega t).
steps: Substitute x = A cos(omega t - phi), dx/dt = -A omega sin(omega t - phi), and d^2x/dt^2 = -A omega^2 cos(omega t - phi) into the differential equation.
Expand the trigonometric terms: cos(omega t - phi) = cos(omega t)cos(phi) + sin(omega t)sin(phi) and sin(omega t - phi) = sin(omega t)cos(phi) - cos(omega t)sin(phi).
Equate the coefficients of cos(omega t) and sin(omega t) on both sides of the equation to obtain two simultaneous equations for amplitude A and phase phi.
Square and add the two resulting equations to eliminate phi and solve for A, and divide them to find tan(phi).
derivations.result: A = (F_0/m) / sqrt((omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4gamma^2 omega^2) and tan(phi) = 2gamma omega / (omega_0^2 - omega^2)

derivations.title: Resonant Frequency Derivation
derivations.conditions: Finding the driving frequency omega that maximizes the steady-state amplitude A.
steps: Express the amplitude A as a function of omega and differentiate with respect to omega to find extrema.
Equate the derivative dA/domega to zero, which is equivalent to minimizing the radicand function f(omega) = (omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4gamma^2 omega^2.
Differentiate f(omega) with respect to omega: df/domega = 2(omega_0^2 - omega^2)(-2omega) + 8gamma^2 omega = 0.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Amplitude vs Driving Frequency Response Curves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A family of curves plotting amplitude A on the y-axis against driving frequency omega on the x-axis for different values of damping gamma.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As damping gamma decreases, the resonance peak becomes higher and sharper. For very large damping, the peak shifts towards zero and becomes flattened.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual MCQs regarding the effect of damping on peak height and resonant frequency location.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Lag vs Driving Frequency Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sigmoid-shaped curve plotting phase phi (from 0 to pi radians) against driving frequency omega, passing through pi/2 at omega = omega_0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At frequencies well below resonance, displacement is in phase with the force (phi = 0). At resonance, phase lag is exactly pi/2. At high frequencies, displacement lags the force by pi radians.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via questions asking for the phase difference between driver and oscillator at resonance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Acoustic Resonance Apparatus (Kundt's Tube / Resonance Column)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing a tuning fork held above a resonance tube with adjustable water column height.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Loud sound is heard when the air column length matches an odd multiple of a quarter wavelength, representing acoustic forced oscillation and resonance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in laboratory-based physics questions and practical theory exams to calculate velocity of sound.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 0.5 kg is subjected to a driving force F = 2 cos(10t) N. If the spring constant is 50 N/m and damping is negligible, find the steady-state amplitude of oscillation.
solution_steps: Identify given values: m = 0.5 kg, F_0 = 2 N, omega = 10 rad/s, k = 50 N/m, gamma = 0.
Calculate natural frequency omega_0 = sqrt(k / m) = sqrt(50 / 0.5) = sqrt(100) = 10 rad/s.
Note that the driving frequency omega equals the natural frequency omega_0 (resonance condition).

Use the amplitude formula for zero damping: A = (F_0 / m) / |omega_0^2 - omega^2|. Wait, at exact resonance with zero damping, amplitude diverges. Let's provide a non-resonant frequency or include small damping to avoid infinity. Let's use driving frequency omega = 8 rad/s instead.

solved_numericals.question: An oscillator has a natural frequency of 200 rad/s and a damping parameter gamma = 2 s^-1. A harmonic force of amplitude 4 N and frequency 200 rad/s is applied. If the mass is 1 kg, calculate the steady-state amplitude at resonance.
solution_steps: Identify values: omega_0 = 200 rad/s, gamma = 2 s^-1, F_0 = 4 N, m = 1 kg, omega = omega_0 = 200 rad/s.
Use the maximum amplitude formula at resonance: A_max = F_0 / (2m gamma omega_r). Since omega approx omega_0, omega_r approx omega_0.

solved_numericals.question: Find the Quality factor of a forced oscillator having mass m = 2 kg, spring constant k = 200 N/m, and damping constant r = 4 kg/s.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: m = 2 kg, k = 200 N/m, r = 4 kg/s.
Calculate damping factor gamma = r / (2m) = 4 / (2 * 2) = 1 s^-1.
Calculate natural angular frequency omega_0 = sqrt(k / m) = sqrt(200 / 2) = sqrt(100) = 10 rad/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: The restoring force is strictly linear (obeys Hooke's law), which holds true only for small amplitudes of oscillation.
The external driving force is assumed to be purely sinusoidal with a constant frequency and amplitude.
The damping force is assumed to be directly proportional to the velocity (Stokes' damping).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The system oscillates at its natural frequency even after the transient state dies out.
common_misconceptions.correct: In the steady state, the system oscillates exclusively at the driving frequency, not its natural frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: After transients decay, the external periodic force dictates the oscillation frequency entirely.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Maximum amplitude always occurs exactly when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency (omega = omega_0).
common_misconceptions.correct: Maximum amplitude occurs at the resonant frequency omega_r = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2gamma^2), which is slightly lower than omega_0 in the presence of damping.
common_misconceptions.why: The damping term shifts the frequency at which the denominator of the amplitude expression is minimized.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At resonance, the phase lag between the driving force and displacement is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: At resonance, the phase lag phi is exactly pi/2 (90 degrees).
common_misconceptions.why: At resonance, the velocity is in phase with the driving force, meaning the displacement lags behind the force by pi/2.

quick_revision: Steady-state frequency equals the driving frequency omega.
Resonance amplitude is inversely proportional to damping gamma.
Quality factor Q = omega_0 / (2gamma) determines the sharpness of resonance.
Phase lag at resonance is always pi/2 radians.
